question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the number is 5. With the U face already visible during PLL, the non-top-facing stickers on the U-layer edges and corners encode the permutation information. In most cases four of those side stickers (e.g., the two visible on the front face and two on the right) are enough to narrow things down, but the two N-perms and the G-perms share enough visual overlap that a fifth sticker is required to eliminate the remaining ambiguity and guarantee you can name the exact case every time.

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer here is 5. In PLL recognition under CFOP you normally need to distinguish both corner permutation and edge permutation from the four side faces. Each of the four edges contributes one visible side sticker and the four corners contribute two each, but you can usually resolve the full case by inspecting a combination that totals five of those stickers (for instance, three edge stickers plus two corner stickers that break the remaining symmetry). That set is enough to rule out all 21 possibilities without needing a sixth sticker in the large majority of orientations.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is 5. When recognizing PLL in CFOP you already know the top layer is oriented, so the key information comes from the side stickers on the U-layer edges and corners. There are eight such stickers in total (two per side across four sides), but because of the fixed centers and the fact that a single edge or corner permutation implies the others via parity, observing any five of them is enough to uniquely determine which of the 21 cases you have; the sixth is then redundant. This is why many recognition systems teach looking at five specific stickers rather than a full set of six.

1.text:
In CFOP the OLL step puts the whole U-face in one colour, i.e.

* U = U

so the whole U-face carries no permutation information at all.  The
permutation that remains to be recognised is the permutation of the
eight U-slice pieces in the U layer.

The U layer is made up of

* 4 U-corners.  A U-corner has the U-sticker on top and two side
stickers on the four side faces of the cube,  4×2 = 8 non-U stickers;
* 4 U-edges.  A U-edge has the U-sticker on top and one side sticker
on a side face, 4×1 = 4 non-U stickers.

Hence the U layer contains

8+4 = 12 stickers which are not on the U face.  That is the whole
information that carries the PLL permutation.  Up to a U-turn the
permutation is carried by one side sticker per piece, i.e. 4 edge
side stickers and 4 corner side stickers, 8 distinct side stickers,
and in practice after fixing the rotation about the U axis the
recognition is normally quoted as the six–eight side stickers of the
U-slice that are normally inspected.  In the literal counting the
U-slice is 12 non-U stickers, 8 corners + 4 edges, all of which must
be readable in principle, the usual working minimum being one side
sticker per piece, 8 stickers, i.e. 4 edges + 4 corners.

3.text:
In CFOP the last layer is first oriented.  After OLL the U face is
monochromatic

U = W W W W W W W W W

so the nine U stickers carry no information at all about the
permutation which is what PLL is about.  All of the information that
distinguishes the 21 PLL permutations is carried by the side colours of
the four U–layer pieces which are still visible on the four side faces.
The U layer is

* 4 U–edges : 1 non–U sticker per edge  = 4 stickers
* 4 U–corners : 2 non–U stickers per corner = 8 stickers

i.e. 4×3 = 12 distinct non-U stickers, the top row of F,R,B,L, on the
U–layer.  In the usual description of a PLL you never look at the U
face itself at all, you look at the side colours of the U layer.
Up to AUF the permutation of the four U edges is already fixed by the
four edge side stickers and the permutation of the four U corners is
fixed by one side sticker per corner, i.e. by 8 distinct U-layer pieces.
In particular the whole U face can be ignored and, up to rotation, the
edge permutation can be read off from the four U edge side stickers
alone.  That is the 12 stickers, 8 distinct pieces, that carry the PLL
information; the U face itself contributes 0 bits.

5.text:
In CFOP the U – layer is finished in orientation after OLL so that the
U – face itself carries no information at all.  What is left is the
permutation of the four U–edges and the four U–corners.

A U edge is identified by its one side sticker, the U sticker being
known to be the solved colour, and a U corner is identified by its two
side stickers the U sticker being known.  Hence up to whole – cube
rotation the last layer is described by

* 4 × 1 = 4 side stickers of the four U edges,
* 4 × 2 = 8 side stickers of the four U corners

i.e. by the 12 side stickers of the U–layer itself.  Modulo the
four–fold rotational symmetry of the U–face the fourth corner and
the parity of corners and edges are redundant, so information
theoretically the 21 PLL types are already separated by

4 edge stickers + 3 corner stickers = 7 distinct non–U stickers,

the customary way of stating it being four U–edge stickers and four
U–corner stickers, eight distinct side stickers, twelve in total on the
U–layer.  In a normal standing view that is the three stickers of the
top row of the front face together with the three stickers of the top
row of the right face, six stickers at a time, which is enough to read
off the case after the usual cube rotation.  This is the 12 side
stickers of the U–layer, usually quoted as the eight
information-carrying side stickers, four edges plus four corners, of
which seven are strictly necessary.

2.text:
In CFOP the last layer is solved in two steps. After OLL the U–face is

*U = U*    i.e. the four U–edges and the four U–corners are all
oriented correctly.  The only thing that is still unknown is the
permutation of the eight U–slice pieces.

A U–edge is identified by the one side sticker that it shows on the
four side faces

* UF : the F–sticker,
* UR : the R–sticker,
* UB : the B–sticker,
* UL : the L–sticker,

so the four edge identities are the four edge side stickers.

A U–corner is identified by the unordered pair of its two side
stickers.  In the usual colour scheme

* UFR : F+R,
* UFL : F+L,
* UBL : B+L,
* UBR : B+R,

so that a corner is unambiguously known when its two side stickers
are known.  The U–slice therefore carries

* 4 × 1 = 4 edge side stickers,
* 4 × 2 = 8 corner side stickers,

= 12 non–U stickers, i.e. the whole side of the U–slice.  That is the
complete side information of the last layer.  In recognition the
four edge ids are enough to fix the edge permutation and one
identifying side sticker per corner is enough to fix the corner
permutation up to the global AUF, i.e. the eight distinct identifying
side stickers of the U–slice.  The 12 stickers are the 12
non–U–facing stickers that belong to the U–slice and are the
information that is normally inspected when a PLL is recognised.

Their argument is parity-redundancy / shared visual overlap, e.g. five stickers suffice to rule out the 21 PLL cases, with some examples citing three edge + two corner stickers. This conflicts with the counting above and with the standard description that the four edge side stickers fix edge permutation and one side sticker per corner fixes corner permutation.

No previous private reflection exists. Unresolved tension: literal total 12 vs minimal distinct 8 vs information-theoretic minimal 7 vs claimed minimal 5. The majority of colleagues support the 12 sticker total / 8 distinct identifying sticker description.   - 4 U-edges × 1 non-U sticker = 4 edge side stickers UF, UR, UB, UL
  - 4 U-corners × 2 non-U stickers = 8 corner side stickers
  total 12 non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer, the top row of F,R,B,L. This is the complete physical side inventory that carries PLL.

* Up to whole-cube rotation/AUF the information can be compressed. Edge permutation is fixed by the four edge side stickers. A corner is identified by its unordered pair of side colours; in practice one identifying side sticker per corner is enough for the permutation up to global U rotation, giving 4 edge + 4 corner = 8 distinct identifying side stickers. In a fixed standing view that is six stickers at a time, top row of F + top row of R.

* Dissident claim persists from 4,6,7 in round 4:
  - Colleague 4 argues fixed centres + mandatory edge-corner parity + AUF collapses the 21 cases to any five of the 12 stickers, e.g. three front top-row stickers + two visible right-face corner stickers gives a unique signature for every G-perm, N-perm, J/Z case, and the sixth sticker is forced/redundant.

* Counter-evidence in round 4: Colleagues 1,2,3,5 explicitly reject the five-sticker worst-case guarantee.
  Colleague 1: five-sticker heuristic is not a worst-case guarantee. Edge permutation alone needs the four edge side stickers and corner permutation needs at least one identifying side sticker per corner. Three edge + two corner stickers leave remaining positions under-determined and G-perms, N-perms and J/Z family stay ambiguous on any fixed five-sticker subset without freedom to rotate. Parity and fixed centres reduce the count modulo AUF to the 7/8 figure above, not to a guaranteed five-sticker unique 21-way separation.

  Colleague 3: five sticker worst case guarantee is not sufficient; N-perms, G-perms and J/U/Z family remain ambiguous on any fixed five-sticker subset without freedom to rotate.
  Colleague 5 reiterates literal 12-sticker carrier, operational 8 distinct, information-theoretic 7 modulo AUF, and that parity and fixed centres do not remove the need for guaranteed unique identification.
